stage1.text: In Mat 1:23 the verb whose usual sense is 'to have, hold' stands in the future active, third singular, and carries 'become pregnant' only through the clause it stands in (the virgin, the bearing of a son that follows); the dictionary sense of the code is possession, not conception.

In Heb 11:11 the noun whose dictionary senses are 'foundation, a casting down' is the first member of a two-noun phrase that the verse gives as conceiving; it names the laying down of seed, and the lexicon itself lists 'conception in the womb' for this verse.

In Heb 11:11 the noun 'seed' stands in the genitive, the second member of the phrase that is rendered to conceive (with the casting down, G2602, in the same unit); here it is the male seed, which the lexicon lists for this verse as semen virile.

In Luk 1:31 the verb is in the future indicative, second person, with 'in your womb' and the bearing of a son after it; its sense here is 'become pregnant', one of the senses the lexicon lists for the code (Lk 1:24, 31, 36; 2:21).

In Num 11:12 and Judg 13:3 harah ('to conceive') is said of a woman's bearing of a child: Moses asks whether he conceived the people and gave them birth, a mother's acts set beside nursing, and the angel tells the barren woman, who has not borne children, that she will conceive and bear a son; conceiving is the beginning of the child.

In Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4 harah ('to conceive') is not said of a child: what is conceived is trouble, chaff and mischief, and what is born of it is evil, stubble and iniquity; the verbs of pregnancy and birth are carried over to the devising of harm, the birth being the deed that follows the plan.

In Jdg 13:5, Jdg 13:7 and Isa 7:14 the feminine adjective 'pregnant' is predicated of a woman and followed by the bearing of a son; the word names the state of being with child, and the ESV renders the announcement with the verb conceive.

In Num 5:28 the Niphal (the passive stem, as the morph HVNq3fs shows) of the verb 'to sow' means to be made pregnant, the sense the lexicon lists for the Niphal; the verse sets it as the result for a woman found clean.

In Psa 51:5 the Piel perfect, third feminine singular, of the verb 'to be hot' means to conceive in the sexual sense (the Piel sense the lexicon lists); its subject is the speaker's mother and its object the speaker, so it names the origin of his life.

stage1.text: In Mar 10:42 the participle of the verb 'to think' is used of those reputed to rule the nations; the sense is 'to be reckoned or held to be', a reputation held by others, and not the thinking of the subject, which is where this occurrence departs from the usual sense.

In Mat 1:20 the aorist participle of the verb 'to reflect on' states Joseph's deliberation over the matter before the angel appears; the lexicon's sense 'to revolve thoroughly in the mind, consider carefully' fits, and the object is the circumstances of Mary's pregnancy.

In Heb 11:11 and Heb 11:26 the verb whose first sense is 'to lead' is used of a judgment reached: Sarah judged the one who promised faithful, Moses counted the reproach of Christ a greater wealth; the sense in both is 'to esteem, count, hold to be', the lexicon's 'to think, consider, count'.

In Rom 4:19 the aorist verb of attentive observation has Abraham's own body as its object; the lexicon's sense 'to observe, consider thoroughly, with intense attention' fits, and the verse sets this looking at the facts beside his unweakened faith.

In Heb 11:19 the verb 'to reckon' is in the aorist middle participle and its object is a clause (that God was able to raise); the sense is to conclude by reckoning, reasoning to a conviction on the ground of God's character.

In Rom 4:19 the negator 'not' is stored in the unit of the surface 'considered' but the ESV verse states no negation of the considering: the 'not' in the verse bears on weakening in faith, and the negator sits beside the word, not on it; adjacency is not scope (LX-01). The occurrence is read as the negator it is, with the reach left to the verse.

In Dan 7:8 the Aramaic verb 'to be' (perfect, first person) is not a word of thinking: it stands with the participle of 'contemplate' (H7920) in the same verse and supplies the continued being-at-it of the looking, 'I was considering'; the dictionary sense 'to be, come to pass' is the helper here.

In 1Ki 10:21, 2Ch 9:20 and Neh 13:13 the Niphal of the verb 'to think, reckon' is passive: silver was not reckoned as anything in Solomon's days, and the men were reckoned reliable; the sense is 'to be accounted', the value or standing others assign.

In Pro 17:28 the Niphal imperfect, third masculine singular, means 'is reckoned' (a fool who is silent is reckoned wise); the standing is assigned from outside the person, by what others observe of his silence.

In Job 1:8, Job 2:3 and Pro 24:32 the noun 'heart' is the object-word of an idiom of setting the heart on something (the verbs set or put in the same verses, H7760K and H7896K), and the ESV renders the idiom as considered; the heart is the seat of the attention directed at Job or at the field.

In Ecc 2:11 the Qal of the verb 'to turn' is followed by the preposition and the objects of the speaker's work: the turning is a turning of attention toward them, and the ESV renders it considered; it is a physical verb used of directing the mind.

In Eze 18:28 the Qal narrative form of the verb 'to see' is the first of two acts (he considered, he turned away from the transgressions); the sense is 'to observe, consider', seeing taken in as grounds for the change of direction.

In Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 the verb 'to set, put' (perfect, second masculine singular) is joined with the noun heart in the same units: the idiom is 'set your heart', and it is what the Lord asks of Satan about Job; the physical verb of placing here directs attention.

In Isa 53:8 the Polel imperfect of the verb 'to muse' is put as a question about the speaker's generation: who gave thought to what happened to him; the sense is 'to reflect upon, take to heart', a deliberate musing that the generation did not do.

In Pro 24:32 the verb 'to set, put' (imperfect, first person) is joined with heart (H3820A, id 1281985 in the same verse): the speaker set his heart on what he saw in the field; it is the placing verb of the attention idiom, not a dictionary sense of thought.

In Dan 7:8 the Aramaic Ithpael participle 'contemplate' is the reflecting act of the speaker at the horns, carried with the helper verb 'to be' (H1934) in the same verse; the sense is attentive consideration.

And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, when you have contributed the best of it. But you shall not profane the holy things of the people of Israel, lest you die.’”

stage1.text: In Act 10:21, Act 28:20 and 2Ti 1:6 the noun 'cause' is the ground on which something is done or asked: the cause of their coming, and 'for this reason' in Paul's request to see the Jews and in his reminder to Timothy; the sense is the ground or cause.
In Act 28:18 the noun stands in a legal setting, where the Romans found no ground for the death penalty after examining Paul; the lexicon lists the legal sense 'charge, case, ground for accusation'.

In Rom 15:22 the inferential conjunction 'therefore, for this reason' ties Paul's having been hindered from coming to the work he has just described; it is a connective, read for the cause it states (RG-07), and carries no thinking of its own.

In Jam 3:17 the adjective 'compliant, easily persuaded' describes the wisdom from above in a list of its qualities; the lexicon lists this verse, and the sense is readiness to be persuaded, the ESV's 'open to reason'.

In 1Pe 3:15 the noun whose usual sense is 'word' is the thing asked for by the one who asks about the hope: an account, a reason given; the verse sets it with being prepared to make a defense, so here the word is an explanation and departs from the sense of a spoken word.

In Jos 5:4 and 1Ki 11:27 the noun 'word, matter' stands in 'this is the reason why': it is the matter that accounts for what follows, an explanation of a cause; the usual senses speech and thing are not the sense here.

In Eze 19:10 the stored word is the Qal perfect, third feminine singular, of the verb 'to be', the copula of 'your mother was like a vine'; it is not a word of reasoning and does not render 'by reason of' (which belongs to the preposition and the noun in the clause). The alignment into the unit 'reason' is flagged as a data error (RG-16), not corrected in the reading.

In Job 1:9 and Pro 3:30 the adverb 'for nothing, without cause' stands in the question and the prohibition: Job fears God, and a man is not to be contended with, for no cause; the sense is the absence of ground, which the ESV gives as 'for no reason'.

In Isa 1:18 the verb whose usual sense is 'to rebuke, prove' stands in the Niphal cohortative, 'let us reason together': an invitation to argue the case out between the Lord and the people, followed by what the Lord says; the sense is to set a case before one another, not to rebuke.

In 1Sa 20:29 the adverb 'so, therefore' in the phrase the ESV gives as 'for this reason' ties Jonathan's report that David has not come to the family sacrifice and to his brother's command; it is a connective of consequence.

In Dan 4:34 and Dan 4:36 manda ('knowledge, understanding') is what Nebuchadnezzar says returned to him: in 4:34 when he lifted his eyes to heaven, after which he blessed the Most High, and in 4:36 together with the glory of his kingdom, his majesty and splendor; it names the understanding he had lost and now has again.

In Gen 41:31 and Gen 47:13 the noun 'face' is joined with a preposition and the famine in the phrase the ESV renders 'by reason of the famine': it states the cause of the plenty being unknown and of the lands languishing; it is a prepositional use, not the face.

stage1.text: In 2Cor 5:16 the present verb 'to know' with 'thus' no longer is the second half of the verse's contrast with the earlier regarding of Christ; the sense is to know or size up, now ended as a way of knowing him.

In 2Th 3:15 and 1Ti 6:1 the present imperative of the verb 'to lead, count' has an 'as' complement: do not count him as an enemy, let bondservants count their masters as worthy of honor; the sense is 'to esteem as', a judgment of status.

In 1Cor 4:1 and 1Pe 5:12 the verb 'to reckon' has a person as object and an 'as' complement: in 1Cor 4:1 how the apostles are to be taken, as servants and stewards, and in 1Pe 5:12 Peter's estimate of Silvanus as a faithful brother; the sense is 'to consider as'.

In Col 2:16 the noun 'part, share' stands in a prepositional idiom ('in a part of') that introduces the topics of food, drink, festival, new moon and Sabbath; it means 'with regard to' and is not a thinking word, which departs from the dictionary sense 'part'.

In 2Cor 5:16 the perfect verb 'to know' has 'no one' as object and 'according to the flesh' as its standard; the lexicon lists 'to have regard for one, to pay attention to' for the code, and the verse sets it before the later regard for Christ.

In Exo 5:9 the negative 'not' (used with a verb: let not) stands in the jussive and bears on the regarding of lying words (H8159 in the same verse): the work is to be heavier so that the men do not pay heed; the verse states its reach.

In Psa 28:5 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to discern' is negated and has the works of the Lord as object: they do not discern or give heed to them; the sense is attentive understanding, which the verse says is lacking in the wicked.

In Ecc 3:18 the noun 'cause, manner' stands in an idiom that opens 'I said in my heart': it means 'with regard to' the children of man and is a prepositional use, not a word of thought; it departs from the dictionary sense 'cause'.

In Isa 13:17 and Isa 33:8 the Qal of the verb 'to reckon' is negated and has silver and man as objects: the Medes have no regard for silver, there is no regard for man; the sense is 'to esteem, value', the lexicon's 'to esteem, value, regard'.

In Job 9:21, Psa 144:3 and Pro 12:10 the verb 'to know' means to take knowing account of someone with care: the speaker does not regard himself, the Lord regards man, and the righteous regards the life of his beast; the sense is 'to take note of, acknowledge'.
In Job 9:21 the negative 'not' follows 'I regard' (H3045 in the same verse) and bears on it: the verse states that he does not regard himself; the reach is the verb of regarding.

In 1Sa 25:25 the noun 'heart' is not the speaker's word for a faculty but the object-word of an idiom of setting the heart on someone, in the plea that the lord not take Nabal to heart; the ESV renders it 'regard', and the unit is shared with the verb.

In Psa 74:20, Isa 5:12 and Lam 4:16 the Hiphil of the verb 'to look' means to look upon with regard: in Psa 74:20 the covenant is the object the Lord is asked to look to, in Isa 5:12 the feasters give no heed to what the Lord has done, in Lam 4:16 the Lord's looking on them is withdrawn; it includes both attention and favour.

In Jer 24:5 the Hiphil of the verb 'to recognize' has the exiles as object and 'as good' as complement: the Lord will recognise and regard them as good; the sense is 'to acknowledge, regard', as the lexicon lists the Hiphil.

In 2Ki 3:14 the verb 'to lift' is part of the idiom 'to lift the face of someone', the sense given by the lexicon head 'favour, honour': Elisha says he has regard for Jehoshaphat, which is why he acts; it is respect shown, not lifting.

In 1Sa 1:16 the verb 'to give, put' stands in a plea not to be set as a worthless woman: the speaker asks not to be reckoned as one; the verb of giving is used of reckoning, which departs from its first sense.

In Lev 19:23 the verb 'to count uncircumcised' is a denominative of the foreskin: the fruit of a newly planted tree is to be counted as uncircumcised, which the verse spells out as forbidden for three years; the sense is 'to treat as foreskin, withheld'.

In Deu 9:27 and 2Ch 6:19 the verb 'to turn' is used with a prepositional object of what the Lord is asked to turn toward or not to turn toward: do not regard the stubbornness, have regard to the prayer; it is attention directed, not a physical turning.

In Psa 80:14 the Qal imperative 'visit' follows 'look down from heaven, and see' and has the vine as object: the sense is to attend to and care for, which the lexicon lists for the code (to attend to, look after, care for).

In Deu 33:9 and Job 37:24 the verb 'to see' is negated: in Deu 33:9 the Levite's words of his parents, in Job 37:24 God's attitude to the self-wise; the sense is to look upon with regard, which the lexicon lists, here withheld.
In Job 35:13 the verb 'to behold' is negated and has the empty cry as object: the Almighty does not look upon it; the sense is to take notice of, the lexicon's 'to regard'.

In Job 34:27 the Hiphil perfect of the verb 'to be prudent' is negated and has all his ways as object: they had no regard for them; the sense is 'to give heed to, consider', which the lexicon lists for the Hiphil.

In 2Ch 5:11 the verb 'to keep, observe' is in a phrase about the priests being present without regard to their divisions; the sense is not keeping to the order of their courses, observing a rule, which the ESV gives as 'regard'.

In Gen 4:5, Exo 5:9 and Psa 119:117 the verb 'to gaze at' is used of regard, with its object a person's offering, lying words and the Lord's statutes: Cain's offering was not looked on, the men are not to look to lying words, the psalmist asks to look continually at the statutes.

stage1.text: In Luk 22:24 the verb 'to think' stands in a clause about which of the disciples is to be regarded as greatest: it is the standing assigned to a person, 'to be reckoned', and not what the subject thinks.

In Rom 2:26 and Rom 8:36 the verb 'to reckon' is passive and carries an 'as': the uncircumcised will be counted as circumcision, and the believers are counted as sheep for slaughter; the sense is 'to be counted as', a status assigned.

In Gen 31:15, Psa 44:22, Lam 4:2 and Hos 8:12 the Niphal perfect of the verb 'to reckon' is followed by 'as' and the thing compared: foreigners, sheep to be slaughtered, earthen pots, a strange thing; the sense is 'to be accounted as', the status others give.

In Isa 29:16 and Isa 29:17 the Niphal imperfect of the verb 'to reckon' is in two questions with 'as' and the thing compared (the potter as clay; the fruitful field as a forest); the sense is 'to be counted as', a status turned upside down.

stage1.text: In Rom 2:3 the connective 'but, and' opens the question with the verb of reckoning (G3049 in the same verse), so that the sentence runs on from the accusation of 2:1; it is read as a connective, not as a word of supposing.

In Jam 4:5 the present verb 'to think' stands in a question put to the readers: do you suppose that the Scripture speaks to no purpose; the sense is 'to suppose, imagine', set in a rhetorical question.

In Joh 21:25 and Jam 1:7 the present verb 'to suppose' is set in the first person (the writer's estimate that the world could not contain the books) and in a third-person prohibition (that person must not suppose he will receive); the sense is 'to suppose, expect'.

In Luk 7:43 and Act 2:15 the verb 'to take up, suppose' is used of a considered view: Simon's answer 'I suppose' and the charge of drunkenness 'as you suppose'; the sense is 'to take it that', an assumption offered.
In Act 13:25 the present verb 'to suppose, suspect' is in Paul's quotation of John: what do you suppose that I am; the sense is 'to suspect, take to be'.

In Gen 18:28-32 the adverb 'perhaps' is the word with which Abraham sets a conceivable number of righteous to the Lord, five times with the number falling from forty-five to ten; it introduces a case put for argument, which the ESV renders 'suppose'.

In 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 13:33 the verb 'to say' stands in 'let not my lord suppose' that all the king's sons are dead: the lexicon lists 'to say in one's heart, to think' for the Qal, and the verse gives the content of what he is not to think.

stage1.text: In 2Pe 1:13 the connective 'now, and' stands in the unit of 'think' ahead of 'I think it right' and turns from the previous verse to the writer's resolve to remind; it is read as a connective (RG-07), not as the verb of thinking.

In Mat 17:25, 18:12, 21:28, 22:17, 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56 and Heb 10:29 the present verb 'to think' stands in a question that asks the hearer for his opinion: what do you think, which of these three do you think; the sense is 'to hold an opinion', asked for.

In Mat 6:7, 26:53, Luk 12:51, 13:2, 13:4, Joh 5:39, Joh 5:45 and Joh 16:2 the verb 'to think' states a supposition or assumption about a state of affairs, often one the verse corrects: that many words will be heard, that Jesus cannot appeal, that he came to give peace; the sense is 'to suppose'.

In 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23 and 2Cor 11:16 the verb 'to think' states the speaker's own judgment or esteem (I think God has exhibited us, we think less honorable, let no one think me foolish); the sense is 'to judge, deem', an estimate of persons or parts.

In Mat 9:4 the present verb 'to reflect on' has evil things as object and the hearts as the place: Jesus asks why they entertain evil in their hearts, so the verb is a sustained inward turning over of a matter, in a verse where he first knows their thoughts (G1761, same verse).

In 2Pe 1:13 the present verb 'to lead, count' is in the first person with the judgment that follows (it is right to stir up by reminder); the sense is 'to consider, hold' something to be right, the lexicon's 'think, consider, count'.

In 2Cor 12:6 the verb 'to reckon' has the speaker as object, set against what others see and hear of him: the worry is the estimate others form of Paul beyond the evidence; the sense is 'to credit, form an estimate of a person'.

In Phili 4:8 the present imperative of the verb 'to reckon' has the whole list of true, honorable, just, pure and lovely things as its object: the readers are to take these into account and dwell on them; the sense is a directed reflection on named objects.

In Eph 3:20 the verb 'to understand, perceive' is set beside asking as the two things that God does beyond; the lexicon lists 'to conceive, Eph 3:20', so the sense is to form an idea of, to conceive in the mind.

In Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34 and Act 17:29 the verb 'to think, suppose' is negated (do not suppose, we ought not to suppose) and names a false assumption the verse then corrects: about Jesus' coming, and about the divine being; the sense is 'to suppose, assume'.
In 1Cor 7:26 the present verb 'to think' states Paul's own judgment about what is good in the present distress; the lexicon lists 'to deem, 1Cor 7:26' for the code.

In Rom 12:3 the verb 'to be minded' occurs in an infinitive series that sets thinking of oneself too highly against thinking with sober judgment; the sense is the measure and direction of the mind's estimate of oneself, the attitude held.

In Phili 3:15 the verb 'to be minded' is in a subjunctive and an indicative in the same sentence: the mature are to be minded in one way, and where the readers are minded otherwise God will reveal it; the sense is the mind-set held.

In 2Ki 18:20, Isa 36:5 and Eze 11:5 the verb 'to say' stands for what a person holds or claims: the Assyrian's question whether words are strategy, and the Lord's naming of what Israel says in its mind; the sense is 'to say in one's heart, to think', the lexicon's Qal sense.

In 2Ch 13:8 the verb 'to say' is a participle in the charge that Israel now means to withstand the kingdom: it states a purpose they hold, not a thought spoken to themselves, which departs from the sense in the other three verses.

In Est 4:13 the Piel verb 'to liken, imagine' is negated and followed by 'to yourself': Mordecai tells Esther not to imagine that she will escape; the lexicon lists 'to imagine, think' for the Piel, and the verse makes it a thought she is told not to hold.
In Psa 119:52 the psalmist calls to mind the Lord's rules from of old and takes comfort: zakar ('to remember') is the recalling of what the Lord has ordained, and the verse gives its effect, comfort.

In Isa 10:7 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to plan' has the heart as subject and is negated, set against what is in his heart (to destroy); the sense is 'to devise, plan', the planning of the Assyrian that the Lord says is not what is in the king's own thought.
In Job 35:2 and Job 41:32 the verb 'to reckon' states a judgment held of a matter: do you hold this to be just, one would hold the deep to be white-haired; the sense is 'to deem, hold to be'.

In Psa 119:59 and Psa 144:3 the Piel and the wayyiqtol of the verb 'to reckon' state a reflection or taking account: the psalmist reflects on his ways and turns his feet, and the psalmist asks what man is that the Lord takes account of him; the sense is 'to reflect on, take account of'.

In Job 6:26 and Jer 23:27 the verb 'to reckon' states an intention or design: Job asks whether they mean to reprove words, and the Lord names the prophets who plan to make the people forget his name; the sense is 'to plan, intend'.

In Dan 7:25 the Aramaic verb 'to think, intend' is joined with changing the times and the law: it states what the horn plans after speaking against the Most High; the sense is 'to intend', a purpose that the verse then says is given into his hand.

In Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3 and Jer 40:5 the noun 'eye' stands in the idiom 'in the eyes of' and the ESV gives it as 'think': whom they think best, do you think David is honoring, wherever you think right; the eye is the standing point of a judgment, so the sense is 'in the view of', not the organ of sight.

In 2Sa 18:27 the Qal participle of the verb 'to see' is the watchman's judgment of what he sees of the running: a conclusion formed from observation; the lexicon lists 'to perceive, consider' for the Qal.

stage1.text: In Rom 1:21 the plural noun 'reasonings' stands in the dative as the sphere in which they became futile, parallel with their foolish hearts being darkened; the sense is 'thoughts, reasonings', their line of thinking.
In 2Cor 12:19 the present verb 'to think' with 'all along' is a question to the readers: have you been supposing that we defend ourselves to you; the sense is 'to suppose'.

In 1Pe 4:1 the noun 'thought, attitude' is the thing with which the readers are to arm themselves as Christ suffered; the lexicon lists 'thought, purpose, intention, attitude' for this verse, and here it is a settled way of thinking.

In Rom 1:21 the connective 'and' joins the becoming futile in their thinking to the darkening of their foolish hearts; it is read as a connective (RG-07) in the unit of 'thinking' and carries no thinking of its own.

In Heb 11:15 the imperfect verb 'to remember, think of' is conditional, with that land from which they went out as object; the sense is keeping something in mind, which the verse says would have given them opportunity to return.

In Phili 1:17 the present participle 'to suppose' states the intention of those who proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition: they suppose or intend to afflict Paul in his imprisonment; the sense is 'to suppose, expect'.

In 1Cor 14:20 the plural noun 'midriff, understanding' appears twice, in the command not to be children in it and to be mature in it; the lexicon lists 'the mind, intellect, understanding' for this verse, so it is the faculty of understanding.

In Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, Neh 6:9 and Psa 64:5 the verb 'to say' introduces what a person says to himself, and the verse gives the thought in direct speech; the lexicon lists 'to say in one's heart, to think', and the ESV renders it 'thinking'.

In 2Ch 32:1 the same verb has no quoted thought after it: Sennacherib invades and 'thinking to win them' states what he intends; it is purpose and not a thought spoken to himself, which departs from the sense in the other seven verses.

stage1.text: In Luk 12:17 the imperfect verb 'to reason through' is followed by 'to himself' and the question of what to do with the crops: the man deliberates inwardly; the lexicon lists 'to reason, deliberate, ponder', and the unit also holds the verb 'to say' (G3004G).

In Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29 and Act 12:9 the verb 'to think' states a supposition formed from what is seen or heard: a ghost, a spirit, rest in sleep, a purchase, a vision; in each the verse shows it to be a mistaken or partial supposition.
In 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25 the verb 'to lead, count' states a considered judgment that something is necessary: urging the brothers to go ahead, sending Epaphroditus; the sense is 'to judge, deem'.

In Act 26:8 the passive verb 'to judge' has 'incredible' as complement: the question is whether it is judged incredible that God raises the dead; the sense is 'to be judged, reckoned to be', an estimate held by the hearers.

In Luk 12:17 the participle of the verb 'to say' is the second word of the unit 'thought' (the verb G1260 beside it): the man speaks within himself, so the saying is inner speech, which departs from the verb's usual sense of spoken words.

In 1Ti 3:7 the noun 'testimony, reputation' is the thing the overseer must have from outsiders; the lexicon lists the reputation sense, and the ESV renders it as being well thought of: it is the estimate outsiders hold of him.
In 2Cor 10:5 the noun 'thought' is the object of the taking captive to obey Christ, set beside arguments and lofty opinions; the sense is the product of the mind, every one of them.

In Mat 20:10 and Act 8:20 the verb 'to think, suppose' states an expectation or assumption on which the person acts: the first hired expected more, Simon assumed he could buy the gift; the sense is 'to suppose, expect'.
In 1Cor 13:11 the imperfect verb 'to be minded' stands between speaking and reasoning as a way of working things out in childhood; the sense is a mode of thinking, the mind-set of a child.

In Jon 1:6 the adverb 'perhaps' opens the captain's hope that the god will take notice of them (the verb of giving thought, H6245B, is in the same verse); it marks a possibility, not a thought of its own.

In Gen 20:11, 26:9, 32:20, Exo 2:14, Jos 22:28, Jdg 3:24, 1Sa 16:6, 18:11, 18:17, 18:21, 20:26, 2Sa 14:15, 14:17, 2Ki 5:11, 20:19, Job 29:18, Psa 94:18, Isa 39:8, Jer 3:7 and Eze 20:32 the verb 'to say' introduces what a person says to himself and the verse gives the thought as quoted speech; the sense is 'to say in one's heart, to think'.

In Gen 31:31, Jdg 15:2 and Jer 3:19 the verb 'to say' introduces an assumption or expectation in an indirect clause: that Laban would take his daughters, that she utterly hated her, that you would call me Father; the sense is 'to think, assume' with the thought stated as what he took to be so.

In Rut 4:4 and 2Sa 21:16 the verb 'to say' states a purpose: to tell the kinsman of the matter, and to kill David; it is an intention held, which departs from the sense of a belief or assumption in the other verses.

In Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to discern' has the steps and the ways as object and sets the prudent and the upright against the simple and the wicked; the sense is 'to give careful thought to, attend to', which the lexicon lists as 'to give heed to'.

In Deu 15:9 the noun 'word, matter' is the thing that might be present in the heart, an unworthy matter that leads to the grudging look and giving nothing; the noun for a word is used of what is held inwardly, which departs from its sense of speech.
In Num 33:56 the Piel perfect of the verb 'to liken, imagine' states what the Lord purposed to do to the Canaanites and will now do to Israel; the sense is 'to purpose, devise', a plan held.
In Psa 48:9 the Piel perfect of the verb 'to imagine, think' has the steadfast love as object and the temple as place: the worshippers have reflected on it; the sense is 'to ponder, think on'.

In Psa 50:21 the Piel perfect of the verb 'to imagine' states the false supposition of the wicked about God, answered by the Lord's rebuke; the sense is 'to suppose, imagine', which the lexicon lists for the Piel.

In Deu 15:9 the verb 'to be' (jussive) is the 'lest there be' of the clause, joined in the unit 'thought' with the noun for the matter (H1697G, same verse); it is the existential copula and not a word of thought.
In Lam 1:9 the Qal perfect of the verb 'to remember' is negated: she did not call her future to mind, which the verse sets before her fall; the sense is 'to remember, take thought of', withheld.
In 1Sa 18:25 the Qal perfect of the verb 'to plan' states Saul's purpose in the bride-price he sets: to bring about David's fall; the sense is 'to devise, plan' with a harmful end.
In Psa 40:17 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to plan' has the Lord as subject and the poor and needy speaker as the one he thinks on; the sense is 'to take thought for', the planning of care.

In Gen 38:15 the wayyiqtol of the verb 'to reckon' states the conclusion Judah drew from her covered face: he took her for a prostitute; the sense is 'to take to be', a judgment formed from appearance.

In Psa 73:16 the Piel wayyiqtol of the verb 'to reckon' states the speaker's attempt to work out the prosperity of the wicked, which he found wearisome; the sense is 'to set the mind to understand', an effortful working out.

In Ecc 9:10 the noun 'account, reasoning' is in a list with work, knowledge and wisdom that are not in Sheol; the lexicon gives 'account, reasoning, reckoning', and the sense is the activity of reckoning.
In 1Ch 28:9 the noun 'thought, device' is paired with plan as what the Lord understands when he searches all hearts; the sense is the thought or device of a heart, known to him.

In 2Sa 3:19 the noun 'eye' is in the idiom 'in the eyes of' with Israel and Benjamin: what seemed good in their view; the ESV renders it 'thought good', and the eye is the standpoint of the judgment, not the organ of sight.

In Jon 1:6 the Hithpael verb 'to think' states the hope that the god will take thought of the sailors so that they do not perish; the sense is 'to give thought, take notice', and the verse sets it after perhaps (H0194).

In Job 12:5 the noun 'thought' in the construct stands for the attitude of the one at ease toward misfortune: contempt for it; the lexicon gives 'thought, idea', and the sense is the opinion of the comfortable.

In Mic 2:8 the Qal participle of the verb 'to return' in the construct with war is the description of the trusting passersby: those who come back from war; the ESV gives it as 'no thought of war', but the stored word is the returning, not a word of thought.
In Amo 4:13 the noun 'thought, musing' with the suffix is what the Lord declares to man; the sense is a person's own thought, laid open by the one who made the mountains.

stage1.text: In Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21 the plural noun 'reasonings' is the first item in lists of what comes out of the heart, before the sins named after it; the sense is the reasonings that issue from the heart as a source.

In Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8 and 1Cor 3:20 the plural noun 'reasonings' is what is known or revealed to another: Jesus perceives and knows what they reason, what lies in many hearts is revealed, and the Lord knows the reasonings of the wise and finds them futile; the sense is the inner line of thought, open to the one who knows it.
In Jam 2:4 the plural noun 'reasonings' is in the genitive of quality, 'judges of evil reasonings': it is the thinking by which the readers make distinctions among themselves.
In Luk 11:17 the noun 'thought' is what Jesus knows before he answers; the lexicon lists the word for this verse alone, and the sense is an inward thought known to him.

In Luk 1:51 the noun 'mind, thinking' is in the dative with the hearts: the proud are scattered in the thinking of their hearts; the lexicon gives the part of the inner person that thinks, whose seat is the heart.

In Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25 and Heb 4:12 the plural noun 'thought' is the inner content of persons that another sees: Jesus knows their thoughts, and the word of God discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart; the sense is 'thought', set with the heart as the place.

In 2Cor 11:3 the plural noun 'minds, thoughts' is the subject of being led astray from devotion to Christ; the lexicon lists 'the heart, soul, disposition' and 'a conception of the mind' for this code, and here it is the readers' thinking.

In 1Cor 2:11 the stored word is the article ahead of the genitive 'of the man', which the ESV renders as 'thoughts'; it stands for 'the things of' the person and is not a word of thought by itself, and its morph is empty in the stored data, which is flagged as a data error (RG-16), not corrected in the reading.

In Eze 38:10 the plural noun 'words, matters' is what comes up on the heart of Gog in the verse: matters arising in his mind, which lead to the evil scheme; it is the noun for things, used here for what arises in the mind.

In Lam 3:62 the noun 'meditation, musing' (construct) stands beside the lips of the assailants and is against the speaker all day; the lexicon lists 'plotting' for the word, so it is the muttered musing of hostile people.

In Ecc 10:20 the noun 'knowledge, mind' with the preposition marks the place of the thought: even in the mind, the king is not to be cursed, set beside the bedroom; the sense is 'mind, the place of thinking' as the lexicon lists.

In Psa 10:4 the plural noun 'devices, purposes' is what the wicked holds with the pride of his face: all his purposes are that there is no God; the lexicon lists 'purpose, device', and the verse gives the content as a denial of God.

In Gen 6:5, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7 (two occurrences) and Jer 4:14 the plural noun 'thoughts, devices' is what the wicked hold and plan: evil continually, schemes to wrong, thoughts against the speaker, an abomination to the Lord, to be forsaken, thoughts of iniquity, wicked thoughts that lodge; the sense is the planned or entertained thoughts of persons, evil in each.

In 1Ch 29:18, Psa 94:11, Pro 12:5 and Isa 66:18 the plural noun 'thoughts' is the thinking of persons as open to God and having a moral quality: kept toward the Lord, known as a breath, just in the righteous, known with their works; the sense is thoughts as the content of the mind that God knows.

In Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Mic 4:12 and Isa 55:8-9 the plural noun 'thoughts' is the Lord's own thinking: his thoughts toward us, very deep, not known by the nations, and in Isa 55:8-9 set against the thoughts of those addressed as higher; the sense is God's purposes and thinking.

In Job 20:2 the plural noun 'disquietings' with the possessive is the subject: his thoughts answer him because of his haste; it is a troubled, restless reflection, a word that the lexicon gives only as disquietings.

In Psa 139:2 the noun 'thought, purpose' (singular, with the speaker's suffix) is what the Lord discerns from afar, beside his sitting and rising; the sense is the speaker's inner thought, known to God.
In Psa 139:17 the plural noun 'thoughts' is God's own, called precious and too vast to be counted; the sense is the thinking of God, set against the speaker's thought of 139:2.

In Dan 2:29 and Dan 2:30 the Aramaic noun 'thought' is what came to the king on his bed concerning what would be, and the thoughts of his mind that Daniel is to make known; the sense is thoughts of the mind, shown to Daniel by revelation.

In Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10 and Dan 7:28 the Aramaic noun 'thoughts' is the subject of alarming the person: Daniel dismayed, the king's color changed, the queen's counsel, Daniel's color changed; the sense is troubling thoughts that disturb.

In Psa 139:23 the psalmist asks God to search him, to know his heart and to try him and know his thoughts: sarappim ('disquieting thoughts') are what stirs within him, set parallel to the heart, and he asks that God himself test and know it.

stage1.text: In 1Cor 14:29 the present imperative of the verb 'to distinguish, judge' is given to the others when two or three prophets have spoken: they are to evaluate what is said; the sense is 'to discern, judge' between the sayings.

In Zep 1:11 the adjective 'laden' (plural construct) describes the traders as those loaded with silver; the ESV renders it as weighing out silver, but the stored word is the adjective of being laden, not a verb of weighing.

In Ezr 8:29 the Qal imperfect of the verb 'to weigh' is the act of weighing the silver and the vessels before the priests, Levites and heads of fathers' houses; the sense is 'to weigh out' for an accounting, a physical weighing and not a mental one.

stage1.text: In Ecc 12:9 the Piel perfect of the verb 'to weigh' is the first of three acts of the Preacher in handling proverbs (weighing, studying, arranging); the lexicon lists 'weigh, test, consider', and here it is a careful judging of each proverb before it is set in order.

In Gen 24:22, Jos 7:21 and Eze 5:1 mishqal ('weight') is a weight: a gold ring of half a shekel and two bracelets of ten shekels (Gen 24:22), a bar of gold of fifty shekels (Jos 7:21) and the balances for weighing the hair in the sign-act of Eze 5:1; in all four it is the weight of a thing, not an act of the mind.
